issues.title: `torch.compile` with `inductor` backend silently drops forward-mode AD tangents (returns `None`)
issues.author: shadow-orange41
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug


When a function is compiled with `torch.compile(backend="inductor")` and called inside a `torch.autograd.forward_ad.dual_level()` context, the forward-mode AD tangent (JVP) is silently dropped — `unpack_dual(...).tangent` returns `None` instead of the expected tangent tensor.

The same function produces the correct tangent in eager mode and with the `cudagraphs` backend.

## Minimal reproduction

```python
import torch
import torch.autograd.forward_ad as fwAD

def fn(x):
    return (x ** 2).sum()

compiled_fn_inductor = torch.compile(fn, backend="inductor")
compiled_fn_cudagraphs = torch.compile(fn, backend="cudagraphs")

x = torch.tensor([0.1, 0.2, 0.3])
v = torch.ones(3)

with fwAD.dual_level():
    dual_input = fwAD.make_dual(x, v)
    out = compiled_fn_inductor(dual_input)
    jvp_inductor = fwAD.unpack_dual(out).tangent

with fwAD.dual_level():
    dual_input = fwAD.make_dual(x, v)
    out = compiled_fn_cudagraphs(dual_input)
    jvp_cudagraphs = fwAD.unpack_dual(out).tangent

with fwAD.dual_level():
    dual_input = fwAD.make_dual(x, v)
    out = fn(dual_input)
    jvp_eager = fwAD.unpack_dual(out).tangent

print("inductor compiled jvp:", jvp_inductor)
print("cudagraphs compiled jvp:", jvp_cudagraphs)
print("eager jvp:", jvp_eager)
```

## Output

```
inductor compiled jvp: None
cudagraphs compiled jvp: tensor(1.2000)
eager jvp: tensor(1.2000)
```

comments.author: kminhta
comments.body:
TL;DR - workaround monkey patch
```
import typing_extensions
sys.modules['pip._vendor.typing_extensions'] = typing_extensions
```
Replace `pip._vendor.typing_extensions` with the package your system is calling

Hoping for discussion around a more elegant solution though

------------

What seems to be happening for us (cc @tanwarsh) is a mismatch in `typing_extensions`. More specifically, it is a mismatch in the `NoDefault` class that is being checked in order to enforce default ordering (see: [typing_extensions.py#L3314](https://github.com/python/typing_extensions/blob/15d48b2122dbb7124a3c3142222bc4647bb8ef4b/src/typing_extensions.py#L3314)).

`ParamSpec` in `torch._inductor.utils` is being imported from `typing_extensions` (see [L43](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/torch/_inductor/utils.py#L43)). 
Which is later set as:
```
P = ParamSpec("P")
RV = TypeVar("RV", covariant=True)

class CachedMethod(Protocol, Generic[P, RV]):
...
```
The order is actually fine from what I understand, since `P` actually isn't set with a default. The error arises when it is time to actually check the parameters for default. For whatever reason, our codebase will actually use the `pip` vendored `typing_extensions` (i.e. `pip._vendor.typing_extensions`) to check. What ends up happening is the `ParamSpec`'s default is set as `<class 'typing_extensions.NoDefaultType'>` whereas the NoDefault that is being compared is `<class 'pip._vendor.typing_extensions.NoDefaultType'>`. These two classes are not recognized as equivalent and so `has_default` gets set to True and `TypeError` gets thrown.

I was never able to create an exact reproducer using torch inductor's params, directly but I think this should be sufficient to get the point across (the has_default line is lifted directly from [typing_extensions.py#L3314](https://github.com/python/typing_extensions/blob/15d48b2122dbb7124a3c3142222bc4647bb8ef4b/src/typing_extensions.py#L3314)):

```
from typing_extensions import ParamSpec
from pip._vendor.typing_extensions import NoDefault
from typing import (
    TypeVar,
)

P = ParamSpec("P")
RV = TypeVar("RV", covariant=True)

types = [P, RV]

for t in types:
    has_default = getattr(t, '__default__', NoDefault) is not NoDefault
    print(f"Type variable: {t}")
    default = getattr(t, '__default__', NoDefault)
    print(f"Type of default value: {type(default)}")
    print(f"Type of NoDefault singleton: {type(NoDefault)}")
    print(f"Has default value? {has_default}")

# Type variable: ~P
# Type of default value: <class 'typing_extensions.NoDefaultType'>
# Type of NoDefault singleton: <class 'pip._vendor.typing_extensions.NoDefaultType'>
# Has default value? True
# Type variable: +RV
# Type of default value: <class 'pip._vendor.typing_extensions.NoDefaultType'>
# Type of NoDefault singleton: <class 'pip._vendor.typing_extensions.NoDefaultType'>
# Has default value? False
```

You'll see that `P` gets marked as having a default value, but it doesn't.

@poedator 
I think you might be running into the same issue, based on this line from your error:
```
File "/conda/envs/main/lib/python3.9/site-packages/yt/packages/typing_extensions.py", line 3019, in _collect_type_vars
    raise TypeError(f'Type parameter {t!r} without a default'
TypeError: Type parameter +RV without a default follows type parameter with a default
```
Idk for sure, but it's possible that your case is comparing `<class 'typing_extensions.NoDefaultType'>` versus `<class 'yt.packages.typing_extensions.NoDefaultType'>`

We found that a workaround for us is to monkey patch `typing_extensions` to ensure it is the same module

i.e
```
import typing_extensions
sys.modules['pip._vendor.typing_extensions'] = typing_extensions
```
(Replace `pip._vendor.typing_extensions` with the package your system is calling)

@shink @malfet 
Swapping `P` and `RV` would probably work, but that is only because `RV` is a `TypeVar` imported from `typing`, so it is properly detected as having no default while ignoring `P`

Wonder if it is possible to import `ParamSpec` from `typing` instead of `typing_extensions`, or if there is a way to dynamically imported from whatever vendored typing_extension is detecting on system in an elegant way.

Guess we could also raise an issue upstream at `typing_extensions` to have a more robust way to detect "NoDefault" from different modules that'll hopefully get quickly adopted into the vendored versions?

I don't have a robust solution at the top of my mind.

comments.author: hauntsaninja
comments.body:
Oh interesting, it's because if you have the real `typing_extensions` and pip's vendored typing_extensions, then this comparison by identity can hold False https://github.com/python/typing_extensions/blob/196082138aebe36af7f5a1d08691b84dab950eea/src/typing_extensions.py#L3296 because the function is monkeypatched onto `typing` here https://github.com/python/typing_extensions/blob/196082138aebe36af7f5a1d08691b84dab950eea/src/typing_extensions.py#L3320 . So if the last `_collect_parameters` to be monkeypatched (by whatever typing_extensions is imported last) is capturing a `NoDefault` that is different from the `NoDefault` set on the ParamSpec you are using https://github.com/python/typing_extensions/blob/196082138aebe36af7f5a1d08691b84dab950eea/src/typing_extensions.py#L1675 , you have set the stage for badness if you trigger it with the right generic class definition!

Minimal repro:
```
import typing_extensions
import pip._vendor.typing_extensions

# minimised torch._dynamo
import typing
P = typing_extensions.ParamSpec("P")
R = typing.TypeVar("R")
class X(typing.Generic[P, R]):
    ...
```

You'll notice that if you swap the import order, it starts working :-)

Upgrading pip works because pip has at least for now seemingly stopped vendoring typing_extensions. Upgrading to Python 3.13 will also solve. Other fixes include not using libraries that use modules vendored by other packages, that's evil. Or if you're really in a pinch, be evil yourself and import pip's internals before anything else executes.

issues.body:
## 🐛 Describe the bug

On Windows (long paths **disabled**, the default), `torch.compile` aborts with a
`FileNotFoundError` for an Inductor-generated `.ttir` file whenever a fused
backward kernel gets a long *descriptive* name. Inductor names such kernels by
concatenating every fused op (e.g.
`triton_per_fused__fused_rms_norm__fused_rms_norm_backward_add_embedding_dense_backward_native_dropout_native_dropout_backward_1`).
The resulting full cache path exceeds the legacy 260-char `MAX_PATH`, so Triton
cannot reopen the `.ttir` it just wrote, and compilation dies.

A trivial pointwise kernel compiles fine, but kernels whose descriptive names
are long enough to cross 260 fail.

### Minimal repro

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class M(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocab=128, dim=32, layers=2):
        super().__init__()
        self.emb = nn.Embedding(vocab, dim)
        self.drop = nn.Dropout(0.1)
        self.gains = nn.ParameterList(nn.Parameter(torch.ones(dim)) for _ in range(layers))

    def forward(self, x):
        h = self.drop(self.emb(x))
        for g in self.gains:
            h = h + F.rms_norm(h, (h.shape[-1],), g)
        return h

m = torch.compile(M().cuda())
x = torch.randint(0, 128, (8, 16), device="cuda")
m(x).sum().backward()
print("OK")
```

Reproduction depends on the *total* path length crossing 260, i.e. on
`len(inductor_cache_dir) + len(kernel_name)`. The snippet above fails even with a
short cache root (`E:\Temp\torchinductor_<user>`, path = **264**); on a default
install (`C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\Temp\torchinductor_<user>\...`, a ~140-char
prefix) much shorter kernel names already overflow.

### Error

```
torch._inductor.exc.InductorError: FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory:
'E:\Temp\torchinductor\triton\0\QJtw5Dl1SLQpes2jQTHSICADfUXY5hnEN4WCy2ss5qI\
tmp.pid_10096_e9cd651e-f7f8-44b8-ab1e-9f34c73e0198\
triton_per_fused__fused_rms_norm__fused_rms_norm_backward_add_embedding_dense_backward_native_dropout_native_dropout_backward_1.ttir'
```

(raised from `torch/_inductor/runtime/triton_heuristics.py` during autotuning)

### Root cause

- Failing path length = **264** (and **283** for the original real-world model), both > `MAX_PATH` (260).
- `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\FileSystem\LongPathsEnabled = 0` (Windows default).
- Switching to short generic kernel names eliminates the long path and compiles fine.

### Workaround

In-process, before the first `torch.compile`:

```python
import torch._inductor.config as ic
ic.triton.descriptive_names = False   # short names -> path stays under MAX_PATH
```

Note: the env-var form `TORCHINDUCTOR_DESCRIPTIVE_NAMES=0` does **not** take
effect here, only the Python config flag works. Enabling Windows long-path
support (registry) would also avoid it but needs admin + a per-process opt-in.

### Suggested fix

Either side could own this:
- **Inductor**: cap/sanitize the descriptive kernel-name length on Windows (or
  whenever long paths are unavailable) so generated cache paths stay < `MAX_PATH`.
- **Triton (Windows)**: have the cache manager hash/truncate the on-disk
  filename, or open with the `\\?\` extended-length prefix, so a long kernel name
  can never produce an unopenable path.

## Versions

- PyTorch: **2.12.0+cu126** (also reproduces on **2.9.1+cu128**; worked on **2.6.0+cu124**)
- Triton: **triton-windows 3.2.0.post21**
- OS: Windows 11 Home (10.0.26200), long paths disabled
- Python: 3.12.10
- GPU: RTX 3060

comments.author: leslie-fang-intel
comments.body: Investigating the regression in `T5ForConditionalGeneration` with @yanbing-j, it appears to be related to buffer realization and reuse. For example, before the regression, one buffer could be reused across the next 6 attention layers without re-computation. However, after the regression, an additional add operation was fused into the Pointwise node, making the buffer non-reusable and causing 6 re-computations. We may need to tune the buffer realization heuristic for this case.

issues.title: `torch.compile` silently returns a result for `torch.linalg.cholesky` on non-positive-definite input
issues.author: rookieLiu2018
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

### Describe the bug

`torch.linalg.cholesky` correctly raises an error in eager mode when the input matrix is not positive-definite. However, when the same function is compiled with `torch.compile(..., backend="inductor", fullgraph=True)`, the compiled function silently returns a tensor instead of raising an error.

### Reproducer

```python
import torch

A = torch.tensor(
    [
        [1.0, 2.0],
        [2.0, 1.0],
    ],
    dtype=torch.float32,
)

def fn(x):
    return torch.linalg.cholesky(x)

try:
    y_eager = fn(A)
    print("eager ok:")
    print(y_eager)
except Exception as e:
    print("eager error:")
    print(type(e).__name__)
    print(e)

try:
    compiled_fn = torch.compile(fn, backend="inductor", fullgraph=True)
    y_compiled = compiled_fn(A)
    print("compiled ok:")
    print(y_compiled)
except Exception as e:
    print("compiled error:")
    print(type(e).__name__)
    print(e)
```
Output:
```
eager error:
_LinAlgError
linalg.cholesky: The factorization could not be completed because the input is not positive-definite (the leading minor of order 2 is not positive-definite).
compiled ok:
tensor([[ 1.0000,  0.0000],
        [ 2.0000, -3.0000]])
```

### Versions

PyTorch version: 2.10.0+cpu

issues.title: [inductor] TypeError: Too few arguments for CSE in cutedsl_kernel.py (torch 2.10.0, Python 3.11)
issues.author: swagglian
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

## Bug Report

### Summary

In `torch 2.10.0`, `torch/_inductor/codegen/cutedsl/cutedsl_kernel.py` references `CSE[Any]` with only one type argument, but the `CSE` class in `torch/_inductor/codegen/common.py` is defined as `Generic[CSEVariableType, AugmentedKeyT]`, which requires two type arguments. This causes a `TypeError` at import time on Python 3.11.

### Error Message

```
TypeError: Too few arguments for <class 'torch._inductor.codegen.common.CSE'>; actual 1, expected 2
```

Full traceback:
```
File ".../torch/_inductor/codegen/cutedsl/cutedsl_kernel.py", line 77, in CuteDSLSubgraphInfo
    cse: Optional[CSE[Any]] = None
         ~~~^^^^^
TypeError: Too few arguments for <class 'torch._inductor.codegen.common.CSE'>; actual 1, expected 2
```

### Root Cause

In `torch/_inductor/codegen/common.py`, the `CSE` class is defined with two generic parameters:

```python
# torch/_inductor/codegen/common.py, line 1886
class CSE(Generic[CSEVariableType, AugmentedKeyT]):
```

However, in `torch/_inductor/codegen/cutedsl/cutedsl_kernel.py`, it is used with only one type argument:

```python
# torch/_inductor/codegen/cutedsl/cutedsl_kernel.py, line 77
cse: Optional[CSE[Any]] = None
```

This internal inconsistency was introduced when `CSE` was refactored to accept a second generic parameter, but `cutedsl_kernel.py` was not updated accordingly.

Note: On Python 3.11, both `Optional[CSE[Any]]` and `CSE[Any] | None` trigger runtime generic type validation, so changing the annotation syntax alone does not fix the issue. The correct fix is:

```python
cse: Optional[CSE[Any, Any]] = None
```

### Steps to Reproduce

```bash
python3 -c "from torch._inductor.codegen.cutedsl.cutedsl_kernel import CuteDSLTemplateKernel"
```

### Environment

- PyTorch version: 2.10.0+cpu
- Python version: 3.11.4
- OS: openEuler (aarch64)
- Install source: official wheel `torch-2.10.0+cpu-cp311-cp311-manylinux_2_28_aarch64.whl`

### Expected Behavior

The module imports successfully without any `TypeError`.

### Suggested Fix

In `torch/_inductor/codegen/cutedsl/cutedsl_kernel.py`, update the annotation:

```python
# Before
cse: Optional[CSE[Any]] = None

# After
cse: Optional[CSE[Any, Any]] = None
```

issues.title: [TensorSubclass] [torch.compile] Better Error message when tensor subclass metadata guard crashes with non-scalar tensors
issues.author: kshitij12345
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

```python
"""
Repro: tensor subclass metadata guard crashes with non-scalar tensors.

The metadata guard (guards.py:2460) does:
    x.__tensor_flatten__()[1] == original_metadata

For dict comparison, Python does element-wise value comparison. When a value
is a multi-element tensor, `tensor == tensor` returns a multi-element bool
tensor. dict.__eq__ then tries bool() on it, which raises:
    "Boolean value of Tensor with more than one value is ambiguous"

This means __tensor_flatten__ metadata CANNOT contain non-scalar tensors,
though nothing documents or enforces this.
"""

import torch

class WeightedTensor(torch.Tensor):
    @staticmethod
    def __new__(cls, data, weights):
        return torch.Tensor._make_wrapper_subclass(
            cls,
            data.shape,
            dtype=data.dtype,
            device=data.device,
            requires_grad=data.requires_grad,
        )

    def __init__(self, data, weights):
        self._data = data
        self._weights = weights

    def __tensor_flatten__(self):
        # Putting a non-scalar tensor in metadata breaks the guard
        return ["_data"], {"weights": self._weights}

    @staticmethod
    def __tensor_unflatten__(inner_tensors, meta, outer_size, outer_stride):
        return WeightedTensor(inner_tensors["_data"], meta["weights"])

    @classmethod
    def __torch_dispatch__(cls, func, types, args=(), kwargs=None):
        def unwrap(t):
            return t._data if isinstance(t, WeightedTensor) else t

        out = func(
            *torch.utils._pytree.tree_map(unwrap, args),
            **torch.utils._pytree.tree_map(unwrap, kwargs or {}),
        )
        if isinstance(out, torch.Tensor) and not isinstance(out, WeightedTensor):
            return WeightedTensor(out, args[0]._weights)
        return out


def fn(x):
    return x * 2 + 1


# Works: scalar tensor in metadata
print("=== Scalar tensor in metadata ===")
x_ok = WeightedTensor(torch.randn(4), torch.tensor(1.0))
result = torch.compile(fn, backend="eager")(x_ok)


torch._dynamo.reset()

# Crashes: multi-element tensor in metadata
print("\n=== Multi-element tensor in metadata (5 elements) ===")
x_bad = WeightedTensor(torch.randn(4), torch.randn(5))
result = torch.compile(fn, backend="eager")(x_bad)

```

issues.title: `torch.compile` (Inductor) fails on MKL-DNN tensor densify (`to_dense`) with "Cannot access data pointer of Tensor that doesn't have storage"
issues.author: tinywisdom
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

When running a simple model that converts an MKL-DNN tensor to dense (`x.to_dense()`) and then applies an elementwise operation, eager mode works fine.
However, with `torch.compile` (default Inductor backend), execution fails with:
```
RuntimeError: Cannot access data pointer of Tensor that doesn't have storage
```

+ Eager and `backend="aot_eager"` both succeed.
+ The error is reproducible on PyTorch 2.8 .

This suggests Inductor’s handling of `mkldnn` layout tensors is incomplete/inconsistent when lowering `to_dense()`.

## Minimal Reproduction Script
```python
# repro_mkldnn_to_dense_compile.py
import torch
from torch import nn

class MyModel(nn.Module):
    def forward(self, x):
        x = x.to_dense()   # densify MKL-DNN tensor
        return x + 1       # simple elementwise op

def get_input():
    x = torch.randn(4, 4)
    x_mkldnn = x.to_mkldnn()     # construct mkldnn layout input
    assert x_mkldnn.is_mkldnn
    return x_mkldnn

def main():
    model = MyModel().eval()
    inp = get_input()

    # 1) Eager mode
    eager_out = model(inp)
    expected = inp.to_dense() + 1
    torch.testing.assert_close(eager_out, expected)
    print("[eager] OK, out shape:", tuple(eager_out.shape), "is_mkldnn:", eager_out.is_mkldnn)

    # 2) AOT-Eager backend
    compiled_ok = torch.compile(model, backend="aot_eager")
    out_ok = compiled_ok(inp.to_dense())  # feeding dense also works
    torch.testing.assert_close(out_ok, expected)
    print("[compile:aot_eager] OK, out shape:", tuple(out_ok.shape), "is_mkldnn:", out_ok.is_mkldnn)

    # 3) Inductor (default)
    compiled = torch.compile(model)  # backend='inductor'
    out = compiled(inp)              # <-- RuntimeError here
    torch.testing.assert_close(out, expected)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

issues.title: torch.compile fails on MKL-DNN tensor after to_dense() with "Cannot access data pointer of Tensor that doesn't have storage"
issues.author: tinywisdom
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch.compile` fails when compiling a minimal model that takes an MKL-DNN tensor, explicitly converts it to a dense strided tensor with `to_dense()`, and then applies a simple elementwise operation.

The same model runs successfully in eager mode. In eager mode, the input layout is `torch._mkldnn`, and after `x.to_dense()`, the output layout becomes `torch.strided`. However, the compiled path fails during the generated Inductor kernel execution with:

```text
RuntimeError: Cannot access data pointer of Tensor that doesn't have storage
This suggests that the compiled path may not be correctly handling the layout/storage transition caused by to_dense() on an MKL-DNN tensor.
```

### Minimal repro
```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-

import os
import json
import platform
import traceback

import torch
import torch.nn as nn


SEED = 0


class MyModel(nn.Module):
    def forward(self, x):
        x = x.to_dense()
        return x + 1


def my_model_function():
    return MyModel()


def GetInput():
    x = torch.randn(4, 4)
    return x.to_mkldnn()


def print_runtime_info():
    info = {
        "python": platform.python_version(),
        "platform": platform.platform(),
        "torch_version": torch.__version__,
        "cuda_available": torch.cuda.is_available(),

        "mkldnn_available": torch.backends.mkldnn.is_available(),
        "mkldnn_enabled": torch.backends.mkldnn.enabled,
        "seed": SEED,
        "compile_config": {
            "fullgraph": True,
            "dynamic": True,
        },
    }

    print("[runtime]")
    print(json.dumps(info, indent=2, sort_keys=True))


def describe_tensor(name, x):
    print(f"\n[{name}]")
    print("shape:", tuple(x.shape))
    print("dtype:", x.dtype)
    print("device:", x.device)
    print("layout:", x.layout)
    if hasattr(x, "is_mkldnn"):
        print("is_mkldnn:", x.is_mkldnn)


def main():
    print_runtime_info()

    if not torch.backends.mkldnn.is_available():
        print("\n[SKIP] MKL-DNN is not available in this PyTorch build.")
        return

    torch.manual_seed(SEED)

    model = my_model_function().eval()
    x = GetInput()

    describe_tensor("input", x)

    try:
        with torch.no_grad():
            eager_out = model(x)

        describe_tensor("eager output", eager_out)
        print(eager_out)

    except Exception:
        print("\n[ERROR] eager execution failed")
        traceback.print_exc()
        return

    try:
        compiled_model = torch.compile(
            model,
            fullgraph=True,
            dynamic=True,
        )

        with torch.no_grad():
            compiled_out = compiled_model(x)

        describe_tensor("compiled output", compiled_out)

        print("same_dtype:", eager_out.dtype == compiled_out.dtype)
        print("same_layout:", eager_out.layout == compiled_out.layout)

        abs_diff = (eager_out - compiled_out).abs()
        print("max_abs_diff:", abs_diff.max().item())

        is_close = torch.allclose(eager_out, compiled_out, rtol=1e-5, atol=1e-6)
        print("allclose:", is_close)

    except Exception:
        print("\n[ERROR] compiled execution failed")
        traceback.print_exc()


if __name__ == "__main__":

issues.title: torch 2.12 regression: torch.compile thread-local config - even backward thread has separate config
issues.author: dxqb
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Since https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/173568 torch dynamo config is thread-local.
`torch._dynamo.config.cache_size_limit` default is 8, which is quite low if you have a couple of different shapes in a transformer. with `fullgraph=True`, this is a failure. without it, it executes code in eager mode when compilation was intended.

setting this value for each thread still seems reasonable, even though it is a breaking change that wasn't documented, I think. However, not even that is enough because the backward thread, launched by torch internally, has its own dynamo config.

If the breaking change was intended, I think at least the backward thread should copy its dynamo config from the thread that launches it.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

Claude repro:
```
"""
Minimal repro: `torch._inductor.config.combo_kernels = True` crashes inductor
codegen with "Dynamic shape on reduction dimension is not supported" when a combo
kernel groups a *persistent* reduction whose reduction dimension is dynamic.

Run:
    python combo_kernels_dynamic_reduction_repro.py

Expected: prints "OK". Actual: raises during compilation:

    File ".../torch/_inductor/codegen/triton_combo_kernel.py", line 550,
        in codegen_static_numels_sub_kernel
      raise RuntimeError(
    torch._inductor.exc.InductorError: RuntimeError: Dynamic shape on reduction dimension is not supported

Three conditions are jointly required (drop any one and it compiles fine):
  1. combo_kernels = True. The scheduler groups >= 2 independent compatible kernels
     into one ComboKernel (no foreach op needed). Here the two `.sum()`s are grouped.
  2. A *persistent* reduction. inductor's heuristic
     (torch/_inductor/codegen/choices.py: should_use_persistent_reduction) picks
     persistent for a small contiguous (ReductionHint.INNER) reduction. For a dynamic
     numel this branch is only taken when the symbol has a static upper bound <= the
     threshold (64); the torch._check(...) calls supply it. Both reductions need a
     bound -- an unbounded one falls back to a looped (non-persistent) reduction and
     the group no longer trips the assert.
  3. The reduction numel is symbolic (dynamic=True). A persistent reduction emits
     RBLOCK == rnumel as a tl.constexpr, but ComboKernel.codegen_static_numels_sub_kernel
     requires every sub-kernel's reduction numel to be a static int and raises otherwise.

Workaround: torch._inductor.config.combo_kernels = False (the default) compiles fine.

Environment this was observed on:
  torch 2.12.0, torch.version.cuda 13.2, triton 3.7.0, NVIDIA B200 (sm_100), python 3.12
"""

import torch
import torch._inductor.config as inductor_config

inductor_config.combo_kernels = True
# Codegen happens at compile time; a stale on-disk artifact can otherwise mask the
# crash on reruns. Disable caching so the repro is deterministic.
inductor_config.force_disable_caches = True


@torch.compile(dynamic=True)
def fn(a, b):
    # Bound both reduction dims so they stay symbolic but inductor picks a
    # persistent reduction (statically_known_leq(numel, 64)).
    torch._check(a.shape[0] <= 32)
    torch._check(b.shape[0] <= 32)
    return a.sum(), b.sum()

    b = torch.randn(16, device="cuda")
    print("OK", fn(a, b))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

issues.title: Dynamo graph-breaks on raw unbacked SymInt inputs during non-strict FlexAttention tracing
issues.author: sanketpurandare
issues.body:
## Issue

During non-strict tracing, FlexAttention can pass raw unbacked `SymInt` sequence lengths from `BlockMask.as_tuple()` into the nested Dynamo trace for `flex_attention_hop`. Dynamo's `VariableBuilder` currently rejects an unhinted raw `torch.SymInt` input with `Attempted to wrap unbacked SymInt`, even when the value is only used symbolically and no Python branch needs to be chosen from its concrete value.

This blocks tracing FlexAttention in flows that intentionally keep the token sequence dimension unbacked, for example graph chunking / non-strict tracing pipelines where the query/key/value token-grid sequence dimension is unbacked and the `BlockMask` sequence lengths are derived from that same symbolic dimension.

## Repro

```python
import torch
from torch.fx.experimental.symbolic_shapes import ShapeEnv
from torch._subclasses.fake_tensor import FakeTensorMode
from torch.nn.attention.flex_attention import BlockMask, flex_attention

shape_env = ShapeEnv()
seq = shape_env.create_unbacked_symint()

with FakeTensorMode(shape_env=shape_env, allow_non_fake_inputs=True):
    q = torch.empty((1, 1, seq, 8), device="cpu")
    k = torch.empty((1, 1, seq, 8), device="cpu")
    v = torch.empty((1, 1, seq, 8), device="cpu")
    kv_num_blocks = torch.ones((1, 1, 1), dtype=torch.int32)
    kv_indices = torch.zeros((1, 1, 1, 1), dtype=torch.int32)
    block_mask = BlockMask.from_kv_blocks(
        kv_num_blocks,
        kv_indices,
        BLOCK_SIZE=128,
        seq_lengths=(seq, seq),
    )

    with (
        torch.compiler._non_strict_tracing_context(),
        torch._dynamo.config.patch(force_compile_during_fx_trace=True),
    ):
        flex_attention(q, k, v, block_mask=block_mask)
```

## Actual

```text
torch._dynamo.exc.Unsupported: Attempted to wrap unbacked SymInt
  Higher Order Operator: torch.ops.higher_order.flex_attention
  Explanation: Unbacked SymInt input is not supported yet.

from user code:
   File "torch/nn/attention/flex_attention.py", line 2505, in _flex_attention_hop_wrapper
    return flex_attention_hop(*args, **kwargs)
```

## Expected

For branch-free symbolic uses, Dynamo should be able to represent the raw unbacked `SymInt` as a symbolic graph input in the nested trace. If user code actually branches on or concretizes that unbacked value, it should still fail with the normal data-dependent-symbol error rather than silently using an optimization hint as a guardable value.

## Root cause

`torch/_dynamo/variables/builder.py` handles raw `torch.SymInt` inputs by creating a dynamic symbolic input when `value.node.has_hint()` is true. When the raw `SymInt` is unbacked and has no guardable hint, it unconditionally graph-breaks instead of creating a Dynamo-owned unbacked symbolic input for branch-free tracing.
